name: Tsua
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 5 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Mathes, Timothy K. & Andy Monthusi Chebanne. 2018. High tone lowering and raising in Tsua. Stellenbosch Papers in Linguistics Plus 54: 1-16. doi:10.5842/54-0-772 (CC BY 4.0)
catalog_locator: p. 1 (Abstract) and p. 6 (sec. 3 'Tonological analysis and proposed representations', text before Table 1)
catalog_quote: The Tsua language is an Eastern Kalahari Khoe language of Botswana (Chebanne 2014). Tsua tone production displays complex Fundamental Frequency (F0) trajectories. Lexical data show that this language has three tone levels: High (H), Mid (M), and Low (L), with the following surface tone melodies: [HH, HM, HL, MM, MH, ML]. High tones may be lowered when they occur following voiced obstruents, aspirated obstruents or the glottal fricative /h/ in root-initial position, a typologically rare pattern. [p. 1, Abstract] ... We posit three underlying tones, High, Mid and Low, to adequately account for the observed melodies. Thus, the two-level melodies with the underlying tones /H/ or /M/, reflect the multiple association of one tone to two morae in a bimoraic root. For instance, the High-level melody is interpreted as having one H tone linked to the first mora while spreading to the second. The three falling melodies associate sequences of two successive tones, one tone linked to each mora in a root. What is surprising is the lack of a phonological /L/ that surfaces as a Low-level melody LL. The Tsua data set does not have instances of LM or LH either. [p. 6, sec. 3]
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Tsua is a lexical tone language with three tone levels (H, M, L) and six root melodies (HH, HM, HL, MM, MH, ML) carried by the two morae of a bimoraic root; root-initial H is lowered after voiced obstruents, aspirated obstruents and /h/, and H is raised to super-high on the high vowels i, u. No source opened says anything about word stress or accent, so no stress position can be read.
new_statements.exceptions: Tonal: LL, LM and LH melodies unattested in the Tsua data set (p. 7); depression is 'non-systematic' in places (Chebanne 2014: 12). Nothing on stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical tone on bimoraic roots (CVV, CVN, CVCV), elicited in citation form from three elderly female speakers; the paper treats the root as the tonal domain and does not discuss stress, prominence, or phrase-level accent.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog kuaa1238 Southern Tshwa [tyu] covers three dialects: Cua/Cuaa (cuat1240), Kua (kuaa1239) and Tsua (tsua1234). The quoted source (Mathes & Chebanne 2018) describes Tsua (tsua1234), spoken in eastern Botswana, from three elderly female speakers; Glottolog's own record for Mathes 2015 assigns Tsua = Southern Tshwa [tyu]. Chebanne 2014 (saved) covers Kua, Cua and Tsua together and calls them a dialect continuum with G|ui/G||ana. Northern Tshwa (tsoa1238; Fehn & Phiri 2017 saved) and Thabala Tchoe (Pratchett 2020 saved) are related Tshwa-complex lects, not this language.

tone_statements.quote: I argue that in the initial mora of roots, Cua makes a contrast between 4 tone heights: /H, M, ꜛL, L/, and elsewhere maintains a binary contrast between /M, L/. ... Cua’s tonal inventory ... consists of 6 non-depressed categories: ‹HH› /H/, ‹HM› /HM/, ‹HL› /ML/, ‹MM› /M/, ‹LL› /ꜛL/, and ‹LM› /ꜛLM/; further, the phonologization of tonal depression as the insertion of an initial /L/ tone ... yields three depressed categories: ‹dHH› /LH/, ‹dHM› /LHM/, and ‹dHL› /LML/, of which ‹dHH› is marginal. [p. 41] ... to extend his proposal to Cua (a language without lexical stress), I define these positions as follows. [p. 257]

tone_statements.citation: Mathes, Timothy K. 2014. Extreme tonal depressor effects in Khoisan: evidence from Tsua. In Proceedings of the 4th International Symposium on Tonal Aspects of Languages (TAL 2014), Nijmegen, 1-5. ISCA Archive.
tone_statements.quote: Like most Khoisan languages, Tsua incorporates tone for lexical contrast but does not display the mobility of shifting, spreading or floating tones typically found in neighboring Bantu languages. ... Lexical items in Tsua are bimoraic, with tones linking to each mora, resulting in tonal melodies of the form [T1-T2]. Furthermore, I am positing three underlying tones High, Mid and Low: /H/, /M/, and /L/. Nasal consonants can bear tone. Six non-depressed tonal melodies have been observed, as seen in (1). ... a. H-H ... b. H-M ... c. H-L ... d. M-M ... e. L-H ... f. L-L
tone_statements.locator: p. 2, sec. 2.3 'Previous analysis of lexical tone' and sec. 2.4 'Tone melodies' with example (1)
tone_statements.summary: Three underlying level tones (H, M, L) on bimoraic roots; six melodies (H-H, H-M, H-L, M-M, L-H, L-L) backed by a near-minimal sextuplet and F0 traces from 3 speakers; depressors (voiced/aspirated stops, /h/) lower root-initial H ~50 Hz. Reviews Vossen 2013's five classes. No stress or downstep.
